content: Vitamin D deficiency during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, and low birthweight. Previous research has suggested that vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy may reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and low birthweight, but it may increase the risk of preterm birth when combined with calcium. However, the effects of different vitamin D supplementation regimens remain unclear. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects and safety of various vitamin D supplementation regimens during pregnancy. Specifically, the study compared doses of 601 international units per day (IU/d) or more versus 600 IU/d or less, and 4000 IU/d or more versus 3999 IU/d or less. The analysis included randomized trials that assessed the impact of vitamin D supplementation, either alone or in combination with other nutrients, on maternal and neonatal health outcomes. Trials that did not include vitamin D supplementation were excluded, as they were analyzed in a separate review. The review included data from 30 trials involving 7289 pregnant women. Eleven trials were excluded, 16 trials were identified as ongoing or unpublished, and two trials were awaiting classification. The overall risk of bias in the included trials was mixed. The primary maternal outcomes assessed were pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, and adverse effects, while the primary infant outcomes were preterm birth and low birthweight. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. For the comparison of 601 IU/d or more versus 600 IU/d or less of vitamin D supplementation (19 trials, 5214 participants), the findings were as follows: Supplementation with 601 IU/d or more may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia (risk ratio [RR] 0.96, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65 to 1.42; low-certainty evidence). It may reduce the risk of gestational diabetes (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.86; moderate-certainty evidence). It may make little or no difference to the risk of preterm birth (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.69; low-certainty evidence). It may make little or no difference to the risk of low birthweight (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.24; very low-certainty evidence). For the comparison of 4000 IU/d or more versus 3999 IU/d or less of vitamin D supplementation (15 trials, 4763 participants), the findings were as follows: Supplementation with 4000 IU/d or more may make little or no difference to the risk of pre-eclampsia (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.22; low-certainty evidence). It may make little or no difference to the risk of gestational diabetes (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.42; low-certainty evidence). It may make little or no difference to the risk of preterm birth (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.12; low-certainty evidence). It may make little or no difference to the risk of low birthweight (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.70; low-certainty evidence). Adverse events, such as hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia, hypercalciuria, and hypovitaminosis D, were inconsistently reported across trials. However, in general, there were few or no adverse effects reported, and the frequency of adverse events was similar between groups. In conclusion, supplementing pregnant women with vitamin D at doses higher than the current recommendations may reduce the risk of gestational diabetes but appears to have little or no effect on the risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, or low birthweight. Supplementation with doses exceeding the current upper limit for vitamin D does not appear to increase the risk of adverse outcomes. The certainty of the evidence for most outcomes was low due to concerns about bias and imprecision. Vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy appears to be a safe intervention, but future trials should provide consistent and detailed reporting of adverse events. There are 16 ongoing trials that, when completed, may provide additional insights into this topic.
